videos.title: My ASUS AI Agent Computer: Local LLMs, Coding & Agent Demos
videos.description:
https://www.asus.com/microsite/agent-computer/in/?utm_source=official-site&utm_medium=asus-hero-banner&utm_campaign=Powering-Every-AI-Choice
Can you run LLMs, write code, and build AI agents on your own workstation? In this video, I walk you through my ASUS AI Agent Computer and demonstrate local AI workflows—from running models with Ollama to comparing a local research agent against a cloud-based model.

We explore GPU utilization, VRAM, response times, tool calls, and estimated API costs through practical examples. I also demonstrate ASUS Zenni Claw for everyday productivity, including an AI news digest and a slide-generation workflow.

If you’re learning Agentic AI, building AI applications, or exploring a workstation for local inference, this walkthrough connects the hardware with real development tasks.

**⏱️ TIMESTAMPS & TOPICS**

00:00 Introducing my AI workstation  
00:22 Why run AI locally? Local, cloud, and hybrid approaches  
01:57 ASUS workstation hardware tour  
03:25 Ollama installation and local model setup  
04:06 Running and chatting with Qwen 3.5 locally  
06:31 Finding and running additional models with Ollama  
07:09 Generating Python code for a Tetris game with Llama 3.2  
07:34 Checking GPU utilization, VRAM, and NVIDIA-SMI  
08:09 Research agent project walkthrough with Claude Code  
09:26 Streamlit app setup and model selection  
10:07 Local vs cloud agents: facts and calculation task  
11:18 Comparing response times, tool calls, and estimated costs  
12:11 Live AI news research: local vs cloud  
13:17 Timeouts, execution limits, and cost observations  
14:00 Compare-and-compute task and local model considerations  
15:44 Introducing ASUS Zenni Claw  
16:19 Local models, additional providers, and API configuration  
16:46 Work Assistant demo: generating an AI news digest  
18:28 Exploring productivity skills and workflows  
18:51 Trying slide generation about Agentic AI systems  
20:17 Key takeaways: AI agents and the infrastructure behind them  
20:54 Choosing between local, cloud, and hybrid AI  
21:07 Workstation resources and closing thoughts  
21:20 Would you run your AI agents locally?

**💡 WHAT YOU’LL LEARN**

- How to get started with local LLMs using Ollama.
- How GPU memory and model size affect local inference.
- How to generate code using a locally running model.
- How to monitor GPU utilization with Task Manager and NVIDIA-SMI.
- How a Streamlit research agent compares local and cloud models.
- How to inspect response time, tool usage, estimated API costs, and failures.
- How ASUS Zenni Claw approaches everyday agentic workflows.
- Where local, cloud, and hybrid AI can fit into your projects.

The comparisons shown are observations from these specific models, prompts, and settings. Local inference avoids per-token cloud inference charges for the locally executed work, while hardware, electricity, and connected services still have costs.

**🖥️ HARDWARE FEATURED**

- Motherboard: [ROG Maximus Z890 Hero](https://rog.asus.com/in/motherboards/rog-maximus/rog-maximus-z890-hero/)
- GPU: [ROG Strix GeForce RTX 5070 Ti — 16GB GDDR7](https://rog.asus.com/in/graphics-cards/graphics-cards/rog-strix/rog-strix-rtx5070ti-16g-gaming/)
- Power supply: [ASUS TUF Gaming 1000P](https://www.asus.com/in/motherboards-components/power-supply-units/tuf-gaming/tuf-gaming-1000p/)
- AIO cooler: [ROG Strix LC III 360 ARGB](https://rog.asus.com/in/cooling/cpu-liquid-coolers/rog-strix-lc/rog-strix-lc-iii-360-argb/)

**🔗 USEFUL LINKS**

- [ASUS Agent Computer at EliteHubs](https://elitehubs.com/pages/asus-agent-computer)
- [ASUS Zenni Claw — features, download, and device compatibility](https://www.asus.com/content/asus-zenni-claw/)
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/)

**💬 JOIN THE DISCUSSION**

Would you run your AI agents locally, use cloud APIs, or combine both? Share your preferred setup and the workflows you would build in the comments.

Like the video and subscribe for more practical tutorials on Agentic AI, LLMs, and AI application development.

What if you could install your own personal AI agent directly on your laptop and connect it to your everyday workflows? 

The world of AI agents is evolving rapidly, with tools like ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, and n8n changing how we automate tasks and build AI-powered applications.

Now, another open-source personal AI agent is entering the conversation!

In this video, I'll explore this new AI agent, explain its capabilities, and walk you through the process of installing and setting it up on your laptop.

 Why Personal AI Agents Matter

Traditional AI chatbots primarily respond to your questions and prompts.

Personal AI agents can go further by combining AI models with tools, integrations, memory, and task execution capabilities.

Depending on their configuration, they may help with research, file management, coding, planning, and repetitive workflows.

Open-source projects also give developers opportunities to inspect the implementation, customize workflows, and experiment with self-hosted setups.

From n8n Automation to Personal AI Agents

If you've been following my channel, you know we've explored n8n, AI automation, Claude Code, and other agentic AI tools.

This tutorial continues that journey by exploring a new personal AI agent and its potential role in your AI workflow.

We'll focus on the installation process, available integrations, and practical ways to get started.

Important: Open-source doesn't always mean completely free to operate. Some integrations and AI models may require API keys or paid services. Review the agent's permissions before granting access to personal files or accounts.

Who Should Watch?

• n8n users and automation builders

• AI developers and enthusiasts

• Claude Code and Codex users

• Students exploring agentic AI

• Anyone interested in open-source personal AI assistants

VIDEO INTRODUCTION:
Ladies and gentlemen,
Think about what Mastercard actually does. It owns no bank. It holds none of your savings. It lends you nothing. It doesn't even issue the card sitting in your wallet. And here's the surprising part: you've never paid Mastercard a single rupee directly.
And yet, HDFC, ICICI, SBI, JPMorgan, and hundreds of other banks around the world issue Mastercard cards. Today, Mastercard powers payments across more than 200 countries and territories, connecting consumers, businesses, and financial institutions on a massive global scale.
